documents.name: Learn Harness Engineering
documents.description: Explore Learn Harness Engineering's project-based course: compare a baseline, preserve agent session state and verify real outcomes before automating coding work.
documents.introduction:
## What is Learn Harness Engineering?

[Learn Harness Engineering](https://github.com/walkinglabs/learn-harness-engineering) is WalkingLabs' open-source, project-based course about the environment around an AI coding agent: instructions, persistent state, initialization, task boundaries and verification.

The curriculum is aimed at people already working with code and coding agents. It is a learning resource with implementation exercises, rather than a hosted agent service or a promise that a particular model will complete every task.

The official README checked November 1, 2026 lists 14 lectures and eight projects. The projects progressively develop the same Electron application, so learners can connect repository organization, session continuity and verification to working software.

## Who should use it?

The course assumes familiarity with a terminal, Git, a local development environment and basic debugging. Its exercises need a coding agent capable of editing files, running commands and handling multi-step tasks.

You can read the material without that setup, but reading alone does not complete the projects. If you want a zero-code introduction, the implementation requirements are a poor fit.

The repository is MIT licensed and the documentation is publicly readable. Access to a model, coding tool or other runtime can carry separate costs; the course license does not include those services.

## Start with the baseline experiment

Begin with the [official documentation](https://walkinglabs.github.io/learn-harness-engineering/) and the first project, which compares a prompt-only run with a run using a minimal harness.

The repository describes that harness using an instruction file, an initialization script and a machine-readable feature list. Their value comes from whether the agent can start correctly, stay within a task and verify the outcome.

A useful way to evaluate the exercise is to keep the starting application, requested feature and available tools comparable between runs. Record:

- What the agent changed.
- Which commands and checks actually ran.
- Whether the requested behavior works.
- What remains broken or unverified.

These are suggested observation criteria, not measured course results from Findry AI. Do not infer a reliability improvement from the presence of more documentation alone.

## Follow the projects in sequence

The course moves from a minimal harness to an agent-readable workspace, then to continuity between sessions and tighter control of feature scope.

Later projects focus on grounded verification, runtime observability and a complete harness. The final projects introduce automated loops and explicit workflow graphs.

Work through the earlier stages before adding a large autonomous loop. If a session cannot initialize the environment or identify unfinished work, scheduling more sessions repeats that weakness.

For a first exercise, keep the completion target small enough to inspect. For example, define a single interface behavior and the steps needed to reproduce it. A feature list should describe observable outcomes rather than vague goals such as “make the application better.”

## Preserve a restart path

The documented session lifecycle starts by reading repository instructions, checking initialization, reviewing prior progress and selecting one unfinished feature. It ends by recording evidence, updating state and leaving a clean handoff.

When trying that approach in your own project, make the handoff useful to someone who did not watch the session. Include the relevant revision, the checks that passed, a reproducible failure if one remains, and the next bounded task.

Keep project-specific instructions aligned with how the repository actually builds and runs. Copying a course template without adapting its commands can create an instruction file that looks complete but cannot initialize the application.

## Use the audit as a diagnostic aid

The repository includes a shell audit utility. From a reviewed checkout, the README documents:

```bash
bash tools/audit-harness.sh /path/to/your/repo
```

Inspect the script before running it on an unfamiliar workspace and use the path of the repository you intend to assess.

The tool checks harness mechanisms and reports whether its critical checks pass. That is a structural diagnostic, not a replacement for running the application or completing an end-to-end task. A repository can contain expected files while still having broken commands or incorrect behavior.

## Decide what to carry into your own workflow

After an exercise, keep mechanisms that address a demonstrated failure: a reliable initialization command, clearer scope, persistent progress or a check that catches a real regression.

The course also includes reusable resources and a harness-creator skill. Treat those as starting points to review against the needs of your own codebase.

For planning and review workflows, see [Superpowers](https://findryai.com/item/superpowers). For explaining a workflow visually, see [Archify](https://findryai.com/item/archify).

## Official sources

- [Course README and project sequence](https://github.com/walkinglabs/learn-harness-engineering)
- [Documentation website](https://walkinglabs.github.io/learn-harness-engineering/)
- [MIT license](https://github.com/walkinglabs/learn-harness-engineering/blob/main/LICENSE)

Sources checked November 1, 2026. This listing is a documentation-based learning guide; no course project or agent-reliability comparison was run for it.

documents.name: Awesome Gamedev Agent Skills
documents.description: Install game development skills for coding agents, verify router discovery and engine versions, then test one gameplay change with Awesome Gamedev Agent Skills.
documents.introduction:
## What is Awesome Gamedev Agent Skills?

[Awesome Gamedev Agent Skills](https://github.com/gamedev-skills/awesome-gamedev-agent-skills) is an open-source collection of instructions for AI coding agents working on games. The official README checked November 1, 2026 lists 77 skills plus a router.

Its scope includes engine APIs, gameplay systems, genres, asset production and publishing workflows. The router is designed to detect the engine and select relevant skills for a request, instead of loading every playbook into each task.

This is a skill collection used with an existing coding agent. It does not include a game engine, a model subscription or a guarantee that generated code will run.

## Preview before installing

The official installation guide documents this read-only catalog preview:

```bash
npx skills add gamedev-skills/awesome-gamedev-agent-skills --list
```

To install through the same CLI:

```bash
npx skills add gamedev-skills/awesome-gamedev-agent-skills
```

The project documents Node.js 22.20 or later for the CLI. Interactive installation asks which skills and agents to use. Review those choices and the project or global scope before applying them.

A separate Claude Code plugin route is documented in the repository. Choose one installation approach first, then inspect the agent's available skills to confirm the router and intended engine skills were discovered.

For a manual installation, copy each skill's enclosing folder with its supporting references, scripts and assets. The installation guide explicitly calls out the router as an additional skill to include. Copying only selected engine folders does not install the dispatcher.

## Match the existing engine version

The collection covers engines including Godot, Unity, Unreal, Ebitengine, Phaser, PixiJS, three.js, Bevy, pygame, LÖVE, Defold and Roblox.

The repository's version-support document defines authoring baselines for new projects. Those baselines are not instructions to upgrade an existing game.

Before asking for code, identify the version declared by the project and its lockfiles or engine metadata. Include that version in the request. If the agent proposes an API from another major release, resolve the mismatch before accepting the edit.

Engine-specific instructions can be useful precisely because APIs differ. A general “make a player controller” prompt is less assessable than one that names the engine, version, input system and expected movement behavior.

## Try one small gameplay task

For a Godot project, a focused first request could be:

```text
Add a double jump to the existing player controller.
Keep the project's engine version and input actions.
Explain which skills you use, then show how to test
grounded reset, the second jump and a denied third jump.
```

This is a suggested test prompt, not a result observed by Findry AI.

The README's routing example combines a movement skill with a platformer skill for this kind of task. Inspect what your agent actually loads; automatic selection is behavior to verify, not proof that installation succeeded.

Review the diff and run the project with the matching engine. Check the intended mechanic and existing behavior: landing, slopes, input buffering, respawn and interaction with animation where applicable.

## Understand the layers

The catalog separates engine-specific material from cross-engine disciplines such as saving, camera systems, UI, game feel and performance. Genre skills combine those parts for platformers, RPGs, puzzles and other structures.

Workflow skills cover prototyping, jams and shipping. Their presence does not mean a store upload, account authorization or release has happened.

The asset-production workflow emphasizes visual direction, consistent families, normalization and inspection inside the game. Generated sprites or textures still need checks at the actual camera scale, with the intended importer settings and rendering setup.

For performance work, establish a reproducible scene and a baseline before changing code. A generated optimization suggestion is not a measured frame-time improvement.

## Verify more than the skill format

The repository includes a validator for its skill files and documents engine-version review. Those checks concern the collection's structure and instructions.

Your own game still needs its compiler, engine or browser checks. For a feature, test the interaction; for an export, inspect the produced build; for a publishing step, verify the destination result.

Keep the engine and task scope small while evaluating the collection. If the first request loads unrelated playbooks, inspect the router and installation before expanding the project.

## License and related costs

The repository is Apache-2.0 licensed. Engine licensing, model usage, asset-generation services and distribution accounts may have separate terms or fees.

For general multi-step coding workflows, see [Superpowers](https://findryai.com/item/superpowers). Browse [Developer Tools](https://findryai.com/category/developer-tools) for related agent utilities.

## Official sources

- [Project README and skill catalog](https://github.com/gamedev-skills/awesome-gamedev-agent-skills)
- [Installation and discovery checks](https://github.com/gamedev-skills/awesome-gamedev-agent-skills/blob/main/docs/INSTALLATION.md)
- [Version baselines and existing-project rules](https://github.com/gamedev-skills/awesome-gamedev-agent-skills/blob/main/docs/VERSION-SUPPORT.md)

Documentation checked November 1, 2026. No skills were installed and no game build or performance test was run for this listing.
